1-intro.title: What AI Is: Quiz
1-intro.description: Check your understanding of narrow and general AI, the Turing test, the two ways to build AI and how the field developed.

questions.prompt: Which kind of AI exists today?
options: General AI that matches people at almost any task
Narrow AI built for particular kinds of task
Narrow and general AI, in roughly equal numbers
Neither: AI is still only a research idea
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § What Counts as Artificial Intelligence], every AI system in use today is narrow AI. General AI does not exist yet.

questions.prompt: In the Turing test, what does the judge try to do?
options: Read the machine's source code
Tell the hidden machine from the hidden person through typed conversation
Time how fast the machine answers maths questions
Count how many facts the machine knows
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Testing for Intelligence: The Imitation Game], the judge chats with a hidden person and a hidden machine and tries to tell them apart.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between the top-down and bottom-up approaches to AI?
options: Top-down applies rules that people write; bottom-up learns from labelled examples
Top-down is used only for images; bottom-up only for text
Top-down needs far more data than bottom-up
Bottom-up was invented before computers existed
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Two Ways to Build AI: Rules or Learning], the top-down approach applies facts and rules written by people, while the bottom-up approach adjusts a model to fit labelled examples.

questions.prompt: What is an "AI winter"?
options: A period when interest and funding for AI fell after promises were not met
A season when AI systems run more slowly
The name of the first AI program
A test of AI in cold conditions
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § How the Field Developed], funding fell sharply in the mid-1970s and again in the late 1980s, periods now called AI winters.

2-symbolic.title: Rule-Based AI and Expert Systems: Quiz
2-symbolic.description: Check your understanding of expert systems, forward and backward chaining, and ontologies.

questions.prompt: Which part of an expert system decides which rules apply to the current facts?
options: The knowledge base
The user interface
The inference engine
The screen
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Inside an Expert System], the inference engine matches rules against the facts, applies the ones whose conditions hold and records their conclusions.

questions.prompt: Which kind of reasoning starts from a possible answer and asks only the questions needed to confirm it?
options: Forward chaining
Backward chaining
Machine learning
Tokenisation
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Forward and Backward Chaining], backward chaining starts from a goal and turns the conditions of matching rules into sub-goals.

questions.prompt: Why are rule-based systems favoured where safety matters?
options: Every decision can be traced to a written rule
They never need updating
They learn faster than neural networks
They need no experts to build
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Worked Example: Diagnosing the Rover by Hand], every action of a rule-based system can be traced to a specific rule, which is why spacecraft and industrial plants use them.

questions.prompt: In an ontology, what does inheritance mean?
options: Rules are copied from one expert to another
Members of a class get that class's properties automatically
Old facts are deleted when new ones arrive
A program inherits code from earlier versions
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Ontologies and Knowledge Graphs], whatever is true of a class is true of its members unless stated otherwise.

3-neuralnetworks.title: Neural Networks: Quiz
3-neuralnetworks.description: Check your understanding of artificial neurons, weights and bias, training, and layers.

questions.prompt: What does a weight do in an artificial neuron?
options: Stores the final answer
Sets how much one input counts in the decision
Counts how many neurons there are
Measures how fast the neuron runs
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § A Model of a Neuron], each weight says how much its input counts, and its sign says in which direction.

questions.prompt: How does a neuron learn during training?
options: Its weights are nudged a little after each mistake
An expert types in the correct weights
It memorises every example
It deletes the inputs it gets wrong
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § How a Perceptron Learns], after each wrong prediction every weight moves by the learning rate times the error times its input.

questions.prompt: Why are neurons connected in layers?
options: Layers make a network easier to explain
Layers use less electricity
One neuron draws only a single straight boundary; layers combine simple patterns into complex ones
Layers stop the network from learning
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § From Perceptrons to Deep Networks], each layer can bend and combine the boundaries drawn by the layer before, so layered networks learn patterns a single neuron cannot, such as XOR.

questions.prompt: What does the bias in a neuron do?
options: Records unfair decisions
Stores the training labels
Sets the learning rate
Shifts how easily the neuron fires, whatever the inputs
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § A Model of a Neuron], the bias shifts the score up or down regardless of the inputs, so it sets how easily the neuron fires.

4-computervision.title: Computer Vision: Quiz
4-computervision.description: Check your understanding of pixels, convolution filters, convolutional networks and the limits of vision AI.

questions.prompt: How does a computer store a colour photo?
options: As a written description of the scene
As a grid of pixels, each stored as numbers for red, green and blue
As a single number for the whole image
As a list of the objects in it
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Images as Arrays of Numbers], each pixel of a colour image has three numbers, one each for red, green and blue.

questions.prompt: What does a convolution filter do as it slides across an image?
options: Deletes the background
Adds colour to grey areas
Records how strongly each patch matches its pattern, such as an edge
Counts the objects in the image
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Convolution and Filters], at each position the filter multiplies the pixels by its weights and adds them up, giving a feature map of where its pattern appears.

questions.prompt: What do the early layers of a convolutional neural network usually learn to detect?
options: Simple edges and colour patches
Whole objects such as cats
The file name of the image
The camera that took the photo
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Convolutional Neural Networks], early layers learn edges and colour blobs, middle layers learn parts, and late layers respond to whole objects.

questions.prompt: Why might a vision system work less well for some people or conditions?
options: Cameras cannot record faces
Vision systems never use training data
Pixels change colour at night
Its training data did not cover them well
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Convolutional Neural Networks], vision models can fail when conditions differ from their training data and inherit the gaps in that data.

5-nlp.title: Language AI: Quiz
5-nlp.description: Check your understanding of tokens, embeddings, attention and how chat assistants write.

questions.prompt: What is a token?
options: A password for a chat service
A small piece of text, such as a word or part of a word
A type of computer chip
A whole sentence turned into one number
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § From Text to Numbers: Tokens], text is split into tokens, which are whole words or pieces of words, each with an ID number.

questions.prompt: What does an embedding capture?
options: A word's meaning, as a position where similar words sit close together
How a word is spelt
How long a word is
Which language a word comes from
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Embeddings and Similarity], embeddings are learned so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors.

questions.prompt: What does attention let a language model do?
options: Read text one letter at a time
Check facts against a database
Ignore the earlier words
Weigh which other words matter most for understanding each word
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Language Models, Attention and Transformers], self-attention scores how relevant every other token is for each token, so the model can use context.

questions.prompt: Why should you check important facts from a chat assistant?
options: It always uses out-of-date information
It never uses real words
It predicts likely text, which is not always true
It cannot answer questions
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Language Models, Attention and Transformers], language models produce plausible text rather than checking facts, so they can state false things fluently.

7-ethics.title: Responsible AI: Quiz
7-ethics.description: Check your understanding of algorithmic bias, fairness audits, the four-fifths rule and human oversight.

questions.prompt: How does algorithmic bias usually get into an AI system?
options: The AI decides to be unfair
It learns unfair patterns from its training data
It runs out of memory
Its screen settings are wrong
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Where Harmful Bias Comes From], bias rarely comes from a decision to discriminate; it enters through data that records past unfair decisions or under-represents some groups.

questions.prompt: What does a fairness audit compare?
options: How fast the system runs
The cost of the system
The number of programmers
Outcomes, such as selection rates, across groups of people
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Measuring Fairness], an audit compares measures such as selection rates and true positive rates between groups.

questions.prompt: Under the four-fifths rule, when is a result flagged?
options: When one group's selection rate is below 80% of the highest group's
When fewer than four-fifths of applicants are selected
When the model is only 80% accurate
When four people out of five complain
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Measuring Fairness], the four-fifths rule flags possible adverse impact when one group's selection rate is below 80% of the highest group's rate.

questions.prompt: What does "human in the loop" mean?
options: The AI copies a person's voice
A person types every answer
A person reviews and can override the AI's decisions, and is accountable
People are removed from the process
questions.rationale: According to [Lesson § Transparency, Explainability and Oversight], human oversight means a qualified person can review, override or stop the system and answers for the outcome.
